bull_bear.body: Coal India Ltd's strong financial performance and low debt levels provide a cushion against potential risks, but the company needs to adapt to the evolving energy landscape and increasingly stringent environmental regulations
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Balance sheet described as a "Stable capital structure, No significant Change", with the Debt Equity Ratio at 0.12 on both 30.06.2026 and 31.03.2026.
- Book Value Per Share rose to Rs 206.91 from Rs 193.26, the deck's remark being "Increase in Net Worth".
- Cash is building: Current Ratio 1.90 versus 1.86 and Quick Ratio 1.70 versus 1.62, both remarked as "Increase in Deposits"; other income rose on "Increase on Interest on Deposits : Rs 449 Cr".
- Receivables are easing: Debtor Turnover Ratio (no. of months of Gross Sales) 0.79 versus 0.81 on "Decrease in Trade Receivables", with consolidated trade receivables of Rs 15,834 Cr at 30.06.2026 versus Rs 15,985 Cr at 31.03.2026 and Rs 17,356 Cr at 30.06.2025 (stated as before adjustment of unbilled incentive and Coal Quality Variance etc.).
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Large scale of operations allowing economies in scale of production - world's largest coal producer at 768.19 MT in FY 2025-26, nearly 74% of India's total coal output
- Meets about 40% of the country's primary commercial energy requirement
- Large coal resource base
- Geographical spread of operations in India allows proximity to a large and diversified customer base
- Strong financial credentials and substantial operating cash flows supporting mining investment, infrastructure, shareholder returns and strategic initiatives
- Skilled and diversified workforce with experience
- Well positioned to cater to high demand of coal in India
- Consistent track record of growth and strong track record of financial performance
- Strong capabilities for exploration, mine planning and operations, supported by in-house consultancy arm CMPDIL
- Integrated mining capabilities across the coal value chain
- Long-term demand visibility - FSA commitment for power, non-power and bridge linkage of about 793.90 MTPA as on 31.03.2026; operative SHAKTI linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with power sector and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers
- Quality assurance infrastructure - twelve empanelled third-party sampling agencies, auto mechanical samplers at silo loading points, live camera feed; declared-vs-analysed GCV gap of only 56.7 Kcal/kg and final grade conformity of 86% in FY 2025-26
- Digital Online Reconciliation Portal facilitating over 1,600 joint reconciliation statements, reducing disputes
- Evacuation infrastructure build-out - First Mile Connectivity projects of 432 MTY cumulative capacity operationalised
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Business risk from captive and commercial coal mining (Risk That Matter) — CIL's near-monopoly on domestic coal is being eroded by captive and commercial miners. It is formally classified as a Risk That Matter and is also shown as a strategic 'Risk to Value Creation' in the value-creation model. Management's stated response is implementation of SHAKTI 2025, enabling imported-coal-based power plants to obtain domestic coal linkages, encouraging wider participation in coal auctions including foreign bidders, and customer-centric measures to enhance market competitiveness - i.e. defending share rather than pricing power.
- Impact of Nationally Determined Commitments (NDCs) on coal demand and production (Risk That Matter) — The energy-transition risk is explicitly on the RTM register: India's climate commitments could structurally cap or reverse coal demand. This is the existential risk for a single-commodity producer whose entire core business is thermal coal, and it is the stated rationale for the renewable, storage, gasification and critical-minerals diversification. The routed text is truncated mid-sentence exactly where management begins describing its response ('CIL continues to').
- Delay in land acquisition and possession for mining projects, with cost implication for permanent employment (Risk That Matter) — Land is the binding constraint on the 1 BT-by-FY30 roadmap: 4,171.79 Ha must be possessed by subsidiaries just to hit the FY 2026-27 target, and land/R&R delays are cited as a primary bottleneck behind 33 of 124 ongoing projects running late. The stated risk explicitly includes the cost consequence of the permanent-employment obligations attached to land acquisition, which converts a project delay into a structural cost burden.
- Delay in obtaining statutory clearances (Risk That Matter) — Environmental Clearance and Stage-II Forest Clearance gate incremental capacity - EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty and Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land are required for the FY 2026-27 target alone. Forest Clearance delays are named as a primary bottleneck for delayed projects. Clearance timing is outside the Company's control and directly determines whether production targets are met.
- Operational safety risk (Risk That Matter) — Mining is described by management as an inherently complex business where safety remains the foremost priority. It carries both a human cost and the risk of mine stoppages and regulatory action. Mitigation is comprehensive safety audits of all producing mines, Principal Hazard Management Plans, mine-specific Safety Management Plans, Integrated Command and Control Centres across all producing subsidiaries and NEC, AI-enabled video analytics and a Safety AI Analytics Dashboard.
- Cyber security risk (Risk That Matter) — Listed first among the six RTMs and repeated in the SWOT threats and the value-creation risk map. CIL runs SAP as its system of record across mining projects and financial reporting, with an Online Reconciliation Portal integrating quantity, quality and finance data for external consumers, so a cyber event would hit operations, customer settlement and financial reporting simultaneously.
- Risk of unviable underground mining operations (Non-RTM Major Risk) — Structurally important because it collides with strategy: opencast mines contributed 96.67% of raw coal output in FY 2025-26 and opencastable coal is stated to be likely exhausted in the near future, forcing a shift to underground mining where a 50 MT-by-2029-30 vision plan and at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35 are planned. Underground capacity utilisation was 77% versus 88% for opencast. The Company itself flags that these operations may be unviable.
- Critical manpower and succession planning risk (Non-RTM Major Risk) — Named as 'Inadequate Succession Planning leading to shortage of critical manpower' on the risk register and echoed in the SWOT weaknesses as 'ageing work force and skill attrition'. With 2,12,066 employees and a simultaneous need to staff renewable energy, storage and critical-minerals businesses, capability transition is a live constraint; mitigation is training, leadership programmes and lateral hiring.

business.body: CIL mines and markets coal through seven wholly owned coal producing subsidiaries, the directly managed North Eastern Coalfields, and a mine planning and consultancy arm (CMPDIL), operating across India's major coal-bearing regions. It operates across the coal value chain with in-house exploration, mine planning, project development and mining operations, supplying primarily the power sector plus steel, cement and other industrial (non-regulated sector) consumers through FSAs and e-auctions. The Company is concurrently diversifying into renewable energy (solar, wind, BESS), thermal power JVs, coal gasification, critical minerals and rail evacuation infrastructure.

outlook.body:
- Balance three strategic priorities: energy security, sustainable growth, and long-term value creation for stakeholders, while accelerating the transition from a pure coal miner toward a diversified natural resources and energy enterprise.
- Grow core coal production toward a strategic roadmap of about 1 Billion Tonne by FY 2029-30 by optimising output across all subsidiaries and delineating enabling activities - statutory clearances, land acquisition and possession, R&R, equipment procurement and evacuation infrastructure.
- Shift the production mix toward underground mining as opencastable coal depletes - identify and plan large high-capacity state-of-the-art UG mines below 250 m and in environmentally restricted areas, introduce Mass Production Technology, and revive closed/abandoned UG mines under Revenue Sharing Mode.
- Use private sector participation to raise technology and efficiency through the Mine Developer and Operator (MDO) route and highwall mining of idle open-cast mines.
- Strengthen the evacuation backbone - First Mile Connectivity projects, SILO/rapid loading, rail connectivity, and strategic rail JVs/MoUs with IRCON International, Indian Port Rail & Ropeway Corporation and Konkan Railway Corporation.
- Improve coal quality and reduce environmental impact through selective mining, beneficiation and blending, and diversification into clean coal technologies.
- Build a clean energy portfolio - utility-scale and rooftop solar, wind in Rajasthan/Gujarat/Andhra Pradesh, hybrid solar-wind-BESS, delivered via a blended model of JVs with state gencos, tariff-based competitive bidding with PPAs, captive projects on own land, and C&I projects.
- Diversify into coal gasification and coal-to-chemicals via Talcher Fertilisers Limited, Bharat Coal Gasification and Chemicals Limited and Coal Gas India Limited to produce fertilisers, ammonium nitrate and synthetic natural gas, supporting import substitution.
- Enter critical minerals - overseas intermediate holding companies in Singapore and Chile, domestic partnerships, and the Rare Earth Elements block allocated in Maharashtra.
- Retain a balanced conventional-plus-clean energy stance, including the 1,600 MW Chandrapura thermal JV with Damodar Valley Corporation alongside renewables.
- Unlock enterprise value by listing subsidiaries - BCCL and CMPDIL listed in FY 2025-26, with in-principle Board approval to initiate public listing of Mahanadi Coalfields and South Eastern Coalfields - creating focused, independent businesses with greater operational focus.
- Institutionalise R&D and innovation through the National Centre for Coal and Energy Research (NaCCER) hub-and-spoke model, a formal R&D Policy, three IIT Centres of Excellence and international research collaborations, moving from proof-of-concept to TRL-4+ prototypes.
- Deepen customer engagement and quality assurance - quarterly zone-wise consumer meetings, Consumer Grievance Redressal Mechanism, third-party sampling, auto mechanical samplers, live camera feeds, and the Online Reconciliation Portal.
- Grow exploration capability - hydrostatic drilling with PCD bits and 3D seismic survey technology to raise exploration rates and increase the domestic reserve base.
- Build human capability - augment training institutes including IICM, large-scale training of employees and contract workers, leadership programmes with IIMs/IITs, structured succession planning, and lateral hiring for renewable energy and emerging businesses.
- Maintain safety as the foremost priority through comprehensive safety audits, Principal Hazard Management Plans, Integrated Command and Control Centres across all producing subsidiaries and NEC, AI-enabled video analytics and a Safety AI Analytics Dashboard.
- Sustain shareholder returns and contribution to the exchequer as a durable capital allocation stance.
- CIL's stated capital-allocation posture is a consistent, high dividend distribution alongside continued reinvestment in mining and diversification platforms, funded by substantial operating cash flows. For FY 2025-26 the AGM notice asks members to confirm three interim dividends already paid - H 5.50 per share (55.00%), H 10.25 per share (102.50%) and H 5.50 per share (55.00%) - and to declare a final dividend of H 5.25 per share (52.50%) on equity shares. Value unlocking through subsidiary monetisation is an explicit part of the capital strategy: BCCL and CMPDIL were listed during FY 2025-26, and the Board gave in-principle approval to disinvest 25% of Mahanadi Coalfields and South Eastern Coalfields via OFS alongside a 10% fresh equity issuance; the Government of India separately divested 123,279,566 equity shares through an OFS, taking its stake to 61.13%. Reinvestment intent covers mining project capex, evacuation and rail infrastructure, renewable energy and storage, coal gasification and critical minerals. As a Government Company, the Board's discretion over composition and appointments - and thus over parts of its governance framework - sits with the President of India / Ministry of Coal rather than with the Board. Note: the source text in this routing states the dividend amounts in the AGM notice; the underlying payout ratio and total dividend outflow figures sit in the financial statements and are not reproduced here.
- Transition towards becoming a Net-Zero Energy Company through a diversified renewable energy portfolio; CIL's initiatives support the national target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based capacity by 2030.
- Internal net-zero target of 3,000 MW of solar capacity by FY 2027-28, scaling to approximately 9,500 MW of renewable capacity by FY 2029-30, against 357.65 MW installed to date and about 523.50 MW under execution.
- Structured year-wise renewable capacity pathway: 357.65 MW installed till date (rooftop 34.15 MW, ground-mounted 323.50 MW), progressive 1,338 MW by FY 2026-27, 3,103 MW by FY 2027-28, 8,954 MW by FY 2028-29 and 9,410 MW by FY 2029-30 (final-year addition via RFS participation).
- Complete saturation of rooftop solar installations across eligible administrative, residential and operational buildings under PM Surya Ghar Yojana - 35.19 MW installed against an assigned target of 34.03 MW.
- Battery Energy Storage System commitments totalling 267.5 MW / 1,070 MWh via BESPAs (187.5 MW / 750 MWh with TGGENCO and 80 MW / 320 MWh with GRIDCO), plus a 600 MW solar project won at Jalaun Solar Park through NHPC's competitive bidding.
- Wind energy portfolio initiated in wind-rich regions - Rajasthan, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh - and hybrid solar-wind-BESS being explored to expand the capacity pipeline.
- Dedicated Renewable Energy Division established at headquarters to steer the clean-energy transition, with CMPDIL acting as project management consultant for site development, DPR preparation and technical vetting across subsidiaries.
- R&D thrust areas formally include Environment, Ecology, Conservation and Sustainability; Coal Mining Waste to Wealth; Renewable Energy; and Clean Coal Technologies, Coal Beneficiation and Mineral Processing, alongside AI/ML/IoT-based smart mining.
- A comprehensive 'Policy & Guidelines on Research & Development (R&D) Projects Funded by Coal India Limited' approved by the CIL Board on 12.02.2026, with NaCCER (National Centre for Coal & Energy Research, Phase-1 established at CMPDIL on 7th October 2024) designated nodal agency and constituted as an independent CIL-funded unit with a Board of Governors headed by Chairman, CIL.
- Three Centres of Excellence for R&D and innovation: IIT (ISM) Dhanbad for Mining 4.0, IIT Hyderabad for Clean Coal Technologies and Net Zero, and a new Centre for Sustainable Energy at IIT Madras with an approved outlay of H 87.90 Crores over 5 years covering sustainable materials and circular economy, mine repurposing and fleet electrification, environmental remediation and pollution control, and materials for energy transition from coal.
- Applied-research prioritisation at Technology Readiness Level (TRL)-4 and above, with projects in Paste Fill Mining in UG Mines, Dry-Beneficiation of Coal, a pilot plant for Coated Spherical Purified Graphite (CSPG), and Surface Hydrokinetic-Based Pumped Storage (SHK-PSP) technology.
- Zero-tolerance Anti-Sexual Harassment Policy under the POSH Act 2013, with Internal Committees constituted at CIL Headquarters and across all subsidiary companies, protection extended to permanent, contractual, temporary and trainee women employees, and guidelines published in English, Hindi and relevant regional languages. Two awareness/workshop/training programmes were conducted during FY 2025-26.
- POSH case disclosure for CIL HQ in FY 2025-26 is a STATED NIL on all three counts - complaints received NIL, complaints disposed NIL, cases pending more than 90 days NIL - and the IC has submitted its annual report to the District Officer.
- Compliance with the Maternity Benefit Act 1961 and the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 by CIL and its subsidiaries, with measures underway to align provisions with Chapter VI of the Code on Social Security, 2020.
- Enterprise Risk Management framework revised and approved by the Board at its 483rd meeting on 8th October 2025, with a Chief Risk Officer operating under a Board Risk Management Committee, named risk owners and mitigation-plan owners, and risks prioritised as six Risks That Matter and four Non-RTM Major Risks as on 31st March 2026.
- Internal control architecture including a documented delegation of powers, operating manuals for all key functional areas, a whistle-blower policy, SAP-based audit trails, an Internal Financial Control checklist covering financial reporting, an independent Internal Audit Department supplemented by independent professional firms performing risk-based audits, Audit Committee review, and C&AG audit plus propriety audit.
- Human capital: 2,12,066 employees, with 3,315 employees trained on health and safety and 12,530 trained on skill upgradation during the year.
- Community investment: H 1,016 Crores of CSR expenditure across 212 CSR initiatives during FY 2025-26.
- Natural capital disclosure for FY 2025-26: 357 MW renewable capacity, 3,161 lakh kL water consumption and 15,94,090 GJ fuel consumption, across 295 mines and 13 washeries.
- Remuneration transparency note: no employee of the corporation received a total remuneration package exceeding the H 1.02 Crores threshold in FY 2025-26. Section 197 and Section 134(3)(e) disclosures are exempt for a Government Company, so the director-to-median-employee remuneration ratio is not disclosed.

outlook.body: Coal India's expansion programme runs on four tracks: core mining capacity, evacuation infrastructure, renewables/storage, and diversification into thermal, gasification and critical minerals. On mining, 124 ongoing coal projects costing more than H 20 Crores are under implementation as at 31st March 2026, with total capacity of 1,044.79 MTY and capital of H 1,69,452.25 Crores - 91 on schedule and 33 delayed, the primary bottlenecks being Forest Clearance, land acquisition/possession and R&R. During FY 2025-26 three coal mining projects were operationalised with 9.0 MTY capacity and a capital outlay of H 936.18 Crores; 13 new mining projects were approved with sanctioned capital of H 13,601.18 Crores and about 77 MTY capacity (about 22 MTY incremental), plus 3 non-mining rail projects with sanctioned capital of H 13,419.95 Crores. New production commenced at 2 MDO projects (20.00 MTY capacity, 1.75 MT produced) and 3 Revenue Sharing projects (4.46 MTY, 0.41 MT produced). The long-term roadmap targets approximately 1 Billion Tonne of coal production by FY 2029-30, supported by 29 identified MDO projects of 254.05 MTPA (Phase-I 15 projects / 172.67 MTPA, Phase-II 14 projects / 81.38 MTPA; 17 opencast and 12 underground), a UG vision of 50 MT from underground mines by 2029-30, at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35, and highwall mining of idle open-cast mines (5 in operation, 4 under implementation, LoA issued for 3 expected to start in 2026-27). For FY 2026-27, EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty, Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land and possession of about 4,171.79 Ha of land are the stated enablers. On evacuation, the First Mile Connectivity programme comprises 72 projects of 843.0 MTY planned capacity with an estimated investment of H 24,600 Crores (the Chairman's spread states H 25,600 Crores), split Phase I 33 projects/379.5 MTY, Phase II 8/55.0, Phase III 17/334.5, Phase IV 14/74.0, with 27 operational, 18 under construction and 27 under formulation/approval; 9 FMC projects of 58.5 MTY were completed during FY 2025-26, and the goal is to expand mechanised evacuation from 151 MTY to 994 MTY. Seven railway projects are under execution - two on deposit basis (Tori-Shivpur New BG Line, 44.37 KM, tripling commissioned March 2024, enabling about 100 MTY from North Karanpura/CCL; Jharsuguda-Barpali-Sardega, 52.41 KM, doubling commissioned February 2024, with flyover complex targeted December 2026 and loading bulbs July 2027 to enhance capacity to about 90 MTY) and five through JVs/SPVs (MCRL Angul-Balram 14.2 KM commissioned, about 15 MTY for MCL; JCRL Shivpur-Kathautia 49 KM at 68.5% progress, commissioning expected June 2027, about 25 MTY for CCL; CERL Phase-I East Rail Corridor 124.7 KM at 96%, balance work by December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL; CERL Phase-II Dharamjaigarh-Urga 63 KM at 38%, commissioning expected March 2027; CEWRL Gevra Road-Pendra Road 135 KM at 80%, commissioning expected December 2026, about 65 MTY for SECL). Project governance has been digitised through the SAP Project System module, with all 124 ongoing mining projects live and integrated with CIL's ERP and the National Coal Portal and IIG-PMG portals. On renewables, installed capacity is 357.65 MW (rooftop 34.15 MW, ground-mounted 323.50 MW), with about 523.50 MW under execution expected by FY 2026-27, including the 300 MW Khavda solar project in Gujarat (200 MW commissioned as of July 2026), 223.50 MW under construction and about 344.25 MW under DPR/feasibility across BCCL, CCL, ECL, MCL, NCL, SECL and WCL. Rooftop solar saturation of 35.19 MW was achieved under PM Surya Ghar Yojana against an assigned target of 34.03 MW. A structured year-wise pathway takes progressive capacity to 1,338 MW by FY 2026-27, 3,103 MW by FY 2027-28, 8,954 MW by FY 2028-29 and 9,410 MW by FY 2029-30, against a committed 3,000 MW by FY 2027-28 internal net-zero target and about 9,500 MW by FY 2029-30. Delivery routes are JVs with state gencos (CIL Rajasthan Akshay Urja Limited with RRVUNL, including 875 MW at Pugal Solar Park; a proposed JV with UPRVUNL in Uttar Pradesh), tariff-based competitive bidding (600 MW awarded at Jalaun Solar Park via NHPC's TBCB), captive projects and C&I supply - including MoUs with C&I consumers for 4.5 GW of renewable power through wind-solar hybrid projects, with planned development of 1.5 GW wind and 3 GW solar. Storage is a new growth area with BESPAs signed for a total of 267.5 MW / 1,070 MWh (187.5 MW/750 MWh with TGGENCO in Telangana and 80 MW/320 MWh with GRIDCO in Odisha). A wind portfolio has been initiated in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, and a dedicated Renewable Energy Division at headquarters steers the programme with CMPDIL as project management consultant. In conventional power, a 50:50 JV with Damodar Valley Corporation will develop a 2 x 800 MW (1,600 MW) brownfield thermal plant at Chandrapura with an investment of H 21,000 Crores. Capacity utilisation in FY 2025-26 was 88% for opencast and 77% for underground mines, with approximately 2,462 million cubic metres of coal and overburden handled, and 2.20 MT of washed coking coal and 6.51 MT of washed non-coking coal produced through washeries.

outlook.body:
- Coal remains India's most significant indigenous energy resource and a cornerstone of energy security, with abundant availability, cost-effectiveness and reliability making it a strategic asset for baseload power.
- As on 31st March 2026 India's coal-based power generation capacity is about 229 GW of a total installed capacity of about 533 GW, i.e. about 42% share, underscoring coal's continued indispensable role.
- Coal is poised to remain a dominant fuel in India's energy portfolio; as envisioned in the Vision @2047 roadmap coal remains pivotal. While growth in coal demand may moderate post-2035, absolute demand is expected to remain steady or increase, driven by sustained baseload requirements.
- Total geological coal resources in India are estimated at about 401 Billion Tonnes as on 1st April 2025 (Geological Survey of India); at the current rate of production the reserves are adequate to meet demand.
- Demand headwind in FY 2025-26: total power generation (incl. RES) grew only about 0.9% to about 1,844.5 BU, coal-based generation fell 3.7% to 1,250 BU and domestic coal-based generation fell 2.3% to 1,174.4 BU. Management describes market headwinds and moderation in coal demand growth.
- Materialisation gap on power-sector demand: FY 2025-26 power sector demand was 668 MT against which CIL supplied 588.01 MT, an 88% materialisation.
- Non-Regulated Sector supply reached 155.5 MT, up 7.0% and the highest NRS supply in any year - a mix shift toward higher-realisation non-power customers.
- E-auction volumes rose to 101.72 MT from 89.38 MT, but the e-auction premium narrowed to 46% from 48% - a realisation headwind despite higher volume.
- Long-term contracted demand base: FSA commitment for power, non-power and bridge linkage of about 793.90 MTPA as on 31.03.2026; SHAKTI and revised SHAKTI operative linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with power and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers.
- Ministry of Coal demand for CIL coal from the power sector for FY 2026-27 is 669.80 MT.
- New demand pools management intends to tap: more coking coal to the steel sector and coal supply to upcoming coal gasification projects.
- FY 2025-26 dispatch was constrained by incessant rainfall in Q2, railway evacuation constraints and rake availability - evacuation is the stated bottleneck being addressed.
- Cost/quality lever: declared-vs-analysed GCV gap of only 56.7 Kcal/kg and final grade conformity of 86% in FY 2025-26 support realisation and reduce disputes.
- Structural cost weakness flagged in SWOT: higher fixed cost and resultant cost of production; inherent inferior quality of indigenous coal due to high ash content; ageing workforce and skill attrition; absence of indigenous manufacturing support.
- Diversification is being framed as a growth platform - coal gasification, critical minerals, renewable energy, battery storage and power generation broaden the growth base alongside the core.
- CIL's initiatives are aligned to the national target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
- Fuel Supply Agreement (FSA) commitment for Power Sector, Non-Power and bridge linkage at about 793.90 Million Tonne Per Annum (MTPA) as on 31.03.2026.
- Operative SHAKTI / revised SHAKTI linkage of about 643.4 MTPA with the power sector and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers as on 31st March 2026.
- As on 1st April 2026, 124 ongoing mining projects costing H 20 Crores and above, of about 1,044.79 Mty capacity, with sanctioned capital of H 1,69,452.25 Crores, at different stages of implementation.
- 13 new coal mining projects approved during FY 2025-26 with combined capacity of nearly 77 MTY; three coal mining projects completed during the year.
- MDO pipeline: 29 projects identified (15 Phase-I, 14 Phase-II) of 254.05 MTY total capacity; LoA issued for 9 projects of 91.48 MTY; production commenced in 8 projects of 87.73 MTY.
- UG revival pipeline: 32 closed/abandoned/discontinued underground mines identified under Revenue Sharing Mode; LoA issued for 28, agreements executed for 27, production commenced in 3 mines of 4.46 MTY capacity.
- FMC pipeline: 72 projects planned in four phases with aggregate capacity 843 MTY; 432 MTY operationalised as of FY 2025-26; nine FMC projects became operational during the year.
- Renewable pipeline: 357.65 MW installed, about 523.50 MW under execution, 223.50 MW under construction and about 344.25 MW under DPR/feasibility across BCCL, CCL, ECL, MCL, NCL, SECL and WCL (this detail appears in the profile routing; the strategy routing truncates mid-sentence in the renewable section).
- Clearance pipeline required for FY 2026-27 target: EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty incremental capacity under approval; Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha forest land; 4,171.79 Ha total land to be possessed by subsidiaries.

risks.note: CIL's near-monopoly on domestic coal is being eroded by captive and commercial miners. It is formally classified as a Risk That Matter and is also shown as a strategic 'Risk to Value Creation' in the value-creation model. Management's stated response is implementation of SHAKTI 2025, enabling imported-coal-based power plants to obtain domestic coal linkages, encouraging wider participation in coal auctions including foreign bidders, and customer-centric measures to enhance market competitiveness - i.e. defending share rather than pricing power.
risks.risk: Business risk from captive and commercial coal mining (Risk That Matter)

risks.note: The energy-transition risk is explicitly on the RTM register: India's climate commitments could structurally cap or reverse coal demand. This is the existential risk for a single-commodity producer whose entire core business is thermal coal, and it is the stated rationale for the renewable, storage, gasification and critical-minerals diversification. risks.note: Land is the binding constraint on the 1 BT-by-FY30 roadmap: 4,171.79 Ha must be possessed by subsidiaries just to hit the FY 2026-27 target, and land/R&R delays are cited as a primary bottleneck behind 33 of 124 ongoing projects running late. The stated risk explicitly includes the cost consequence of the permanent-employment obligations attached to land acquisition, which converts a project delay into a structural cost burden.

risks.note: Environmental Clearance and Stage-II Forest Clearance gate incremental capacity - EC for 8 proposals of about 21.45 Mty and Stage-II FC for 12 proposals covering 2,800.145 Ha of forest land are required for the FY 2026-27 target alone. risks.note: Mining is described by management as an inherently complex business where safety remains the foremost priority. It carries both a human cost and the risk of mine stoppages and regulatory action. Mitigation is comprehensive safety audits of all producing mines, Principal Hazard Management Plans, mine-specific Safety Management Plans, Integrated Command and Control Centres across all producing subsidiaries and NEC, AI-enabled video analytics and a Safety AI Analytics Dashboard.

Listed first among the six RTMs and repeated in the SWOT threats and the value-creation risk map. CIL runs SAP as its system of record across mining projects and financial reporting, with an Online Reconciliation Portal integrating quantity, quality and finance data for external consumers, so a cyber event would hit operations, customer settlement and financial reporting simultaneously.

Structurally important because it collides with strategy: opencast mines contributed 96.67% of raw coal output in FY 2025-26 and opencastable coal is stated to be likely exhausted in the near future, forcing a shift to underground mining where a 50 MT-by-2029-30 vision plan and at least 140 Continuous Miners by 2034-35 are planned. Underground capacity utilisation was 77% versus 88% for opencast. The Company itself flags that these operations may be unviable.
risks.risk: Risk of unviable underground mining operations (Non-RTM Major Risk)

risks.risk: Critical manpower and succession planning risk (Non-RTM Major Risk)

meta.thesis: Coal India Ltd, a dominant player in the Indian coal mining sector, is expected to maintain its strong financial performance driven by increasing coal demand and prices, despite challenges from energy transition and environmental concerns. The company's credit rating has been reaffirmed at CARE AAA with a stable outlook, reflecting its robust financial health and low debt levels. However, the company needs to navigate the risks associated with sustainable mining practices and evolving energy landscape.
